title: Josephine Bakhita (c. 1869–1947)
hookLine: kidnapped in Sudan, enslaved, freed, she became a sister, patron of trafficking survivors

cards: A girl in Sudan is grabbed by slave raiders. She is so terrified that, by her own later telling, she forgets the name her parents gave her. The raiders hand her another name: Bakhita.
She is sold, and sold again. Owners beat her. One has her skin cut in patterns and rubbed with salt, so the scars will stay.
Then an Italian consul buys her, and she ends up in Italy, caring for a family's little daughter. The family leaves the two of them for a while with some sisters in Venice.
What happens in that convent ends with the law in Venice deciding who she belongs to.

teach.b: Start with what she kept. First, the scars. She carried them for the rest of her life, and never pretended the cruelty hadn't happened.
Second, the convent. The Canossian Sisters in Venice taught her about God, and about Christ, who also suffered at the hands of others.
She asked to be baptized. Third, the refusal.
When her mistress came back to take her home, Bakhita said no. She wanted to stay. The mistress pushed, and the case went to the authorities in Venice.
They ruled that she was free: under Italian law, nobody could own her. Fourth, the deeper freedom. She was baptized Josephine, and kept Bakhita too.
Later she joined the Canossian Sisters herself, and for years she cooked, sewed, and answered the convent door in a small town. People came to that door just to talk to her.
Pope Benedict XVI told her story in his letter on hope: after cruel masters, she came to know a different master, one who loved her, and that gave her hope.
In John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "If therefore the son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed." Freed by a ruling.
Free, she said, by being loved.
The Church now names her a patron of people who survive trafficking, the slavery that still goes on.

how: Catholics keep Josephine Bakhita's feast in February, and many parishes and religious orders use the day to pray for victims and survivors of human trafficking and to support groups that help them.

games.q: you're Bakhita, in a convent in Venice. your mistress comes back to take you home with her. what do you do?
games.why: she said no. the case went to the authorities, and they ruled she was free.

practice: Bring to mind the people who, right now, are bought and sold, or who have just gotten out: a worker who can't leave a job, a girl far from home, someone rebuilding a life. You don't need faces; let them be real anyway.
If you pray, ask Josephine Bakhita to stand with them, or hold them before God in silence; if you don't, hold them in your attention and wish them freedom.
